title: FROZEN Capability Universe and Fixed Probe Set — Primary Evaluation 1 (Semantic Compression)
status: FROZEN. No probe may be added, removed, reworded, or re-pointed after this file is written. No capability may be deleted because a language (including Quidra) lacks it.

provenance_and_fairness_statement.derivation: Every probe in this file was derived exclusively from (a) the 20 capability families enumerated verbatim in spec section 6.1.2, (b) the semantic-fact inventory in spec section 6.1.3, and (c) general programming-language theory. No Quidra documentation, source, examples, README, or grammar was consulted. No probe was shaped by Quidra's operators, types, syntax, keywords, or feature set.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.quidra_is_the_subject_not_the_designer: Quidra is the language under evaluation, not the source of the measuring instrument. The benchmark's purpose is NOT to make Quidra score well.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.capabilities_quidra_may_lack_are_retaine: Families 2 (uninitialized state), 4 (writable aliasing), 8 (explicit overflow/div-zero behavior), 14 (closed sum types), 15 (generics with constraints), 17 (deterministic destruction), 19 (concurrency), and 20 (FFI, both directions) are retained in full regardless of whether any particular language supports them. A language that supports them scores higher on Capability Coverage; a language that does not is lowered, per spec 26.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.languages_may_beat_quidra: Nothing in this probe set is constructed so that any one language must win. Probes reward explicit, locally determinate expression of the named semantics whichever language provides it, and penalize hidden behavior whichever language has it.
provenance_and_fairness_statement.no_post_hoc_redesign: Per spec 6.1.7 and 32, this probe set must not be redesigned in response to observed rankings. Any discovered defect is recorded as an erratum in the results, not silently repaired here.

fixed_column_order_note: All downstream tables must use exactly the order above.

toolchain_binding.rule: A probe fragment counts as expressible ONLY if it builds and/or runs under the frozen recipe for that language, with no added third-party dependency and no benchmark-specific code generation step.
toolchain_binding.host: Apple M2, 8 logical CPUs, 8 GiB RAM, macOS 26.4.1 arm64

semantic_fact_kinds._note: Verbatim taxonomy from spec 6.1.3. These 13 ids are the ONLY fact kinds usable anywhere in Primary Evaluation 1, for every language, in every probe.
semantic_fact_kinds.value_vs_storage: Whether the construct denotes a value or a named/addressable storage location.
semantic_fact_kinds.mutability: Whether the denoted entity (and, separately, what it refers to) can be changed after the construct.
semantic_fact_kinds.aliasing_writable_aliasing: Whether two names/expressions can denote the same storage, and whether writes are possible through more than one of them.
semantic_fact_kinds.initialization_state: Whether storage holds a defined value at this point, and if so which.
semantic_fact_kinds.type_and_representation: The static/dynamic type and the concrete machine or runtime representation (width, signedness, boxing, layout, reference-vs-inline).
semantic_fact_kinds.conversion_behavior: Whether a representation/type change occurs here and exactly what it does at the boundaries (truncate, widen, round, trap, saturate, error, reject).
semantic_fact_kinds.possible_failure: Whether this construct can fail, and how the failure is surfaced.
semantic_fact_kinds.alternative_value_cases: Which distinct alternative shapes a value may take here, and whether the set is closed and exhaustively handled.
semantic_fact_kinds.overflow_exceptional_numeric: Behavior at numeric limits and on exceptional numeric operands (overflow, division by zero, NaN, negative modulo, shift overflow).
semantic_fact_kinds.allocation_copy_move_borrow_destroy: Whether memory is allocated, whether data is copied, moved, borrowed, or destroyed at this construct.
semantic_fact_kinds.externally_visible_side_effects: Effects observable outside the fragment (I/O, global/shared state change, OS interaction).
semantic_fact_kinds.control_flow_effect: Whether control may leave, branch, suspend, resume, or not return at this construct.
semantic_fact_kinds.lifetime_resource_effect: When the denoted resource's lifetime ends and when its cleanup runs.

authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments._purpose: These rules make 10 implementers produce genuinely equivalent fragments. They are frozen and identical for all 10 languages.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R1_equivalence: Each fragment must implement the canonical_task's OBSERVABLE behavior exactly. Two fragments in two languages are equivalent iff, given the same stated inputs, they produce the same stated outputs/effects and expose the same stated semantic commitments. A fragment that silently drops a stated sub-requirement is not equivalent and is scored PARTIAL or NONE, not FULL.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R2_idiomatic: Write the fragment the way a competent, current, professional user of that language would write it for production code, using that language's normal conventions. Do not hand-obfuscate, do not golf, do not pad, do not add decorative annotations that a normal author would omit, and do not omit annotations a normal author would include.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R3_minimality: The fragment contains exactly what the canonical_task requires and nothing else: no logging, no comments, no assertions, no defensive checks, no unused declarations, no main/entry wrapper unless the canonical_task names one.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R4_fixed_identifiers: Use exactly the identifier names given in the canonical_task. Where a language's conventions require a different case style (e.g. snake_case vs camelCase), apply that language's normal convention to the same word; do not rename the concept.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R5_measured_fragment_boundary: Each probe declares measured_fragment. Only the text inside that boundary is counted for Semantic Density (tokens and facts), Determinacy, Locality, and Hidden Cost. Supporting context that the probe declares as 'given' or 'declared elsewhere' is NOT counted as tokens but IS counted as a non-local lookup for metric C when a fact requires consulting it.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R6_compilability: Every fragment scored FULL or PARTIAL must be embedded in the minimal compilable/runnable program for its language and must actually build and run under the frozen recipe. The wrapper is excluded from the measured_fragment. A fragment that does not build is NONE unless the probe explicitly asks for a statically-rejected case.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R7_no_external_packages: Standard library and language-bundled runtime only. No third-party packages, no package manager fetch, no code generation, no separate toolchain, no hand-written assembly. Compiler/runtime flags beyond the frozen recipe are permitted only under support rubric criterion P-b and force PARTIAL.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R8_one_fragment_per_probe_per_language: Exactly 400 fragments exist in principle (40 probes x 10 languages). Probes scored NONE for a language have no fragment; that language's record for that probe carries the NONE justification instead.
authoring_rules_for_probe_fragments.R9_no_probe_substitution: If a language cannot express a probe, record NONE with a documented reason. Do not substitute an easier task, and do not mark it N/A (see na_policy).

probes.title: Immutable local binding of an integer
probes.intent: Measure how the language introduces a named, non-reassignable local binding and how much of its value/storage, mutability, type and representation is recoverable from the declaration alone.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body, (1) introduce a local name `n` bound to the integer value 7, using the form the language provides for a binding that will never be reassigned; (2) as the last statement of the fragment, produce `n` as the fragment's result (return it from the enclosing function, whose declared result is the same integer type). Do not annotate the type unless the language requires it or a normal author would write it. The measured fragment is statements (1) and (2).
probes.measured_fragment: The declaration of `n` and the statement producing `n`. The enclosing function header and closing brace are excluded.

probes.title: Module-level mutable storage plus an immutable named constant
probes.intent: Measure how the language distinguishes a long-lived mutable storage location from a fixed named constant, and how much of lifetime, mutability, visibility and representation a reader recovers from the two declarations alone.
probes.canonical_task: At the outermost declaration scope of a single compilation unit (module / file / namespace / class-static, whichever is that language's normal home for such declarations), declare exactly two things: (1) a named storage location `counter`, of a signed integer type capable of representing at least the full 64-bit signed range, initialized to 0, and intended to be reassigned later by ordinary code in the same unit; (2) a named constant `LIMIT` whose value is 100, of the same integer type, which can never be reassigned and which the language treats as a constant rather than as a mutable variable holding a constant value (use a compile-time/immutable constant form if the language has one). The measured fragment is exactly these two declarations. A reader must be able to tell which one is mutable.
probes.measured_fragment: The two declarations only.

probes.title: Declaration without initializer, definitely assigned on all paths
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express 'declared but not yet initialized' at all, and how determinately a reader can tell, at the declaration and at the later read, whether the storage holds a defined value.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a local `v` of a signed 32-bit integer type WITHOUT giving it an initial value at the point of declaration (if the language forbids this, that is the finding — see rubric); (2) write a two-way branch on an already-declared boolean `cond` that assigns `v = 5` in the true arm and `v = 9` in the false arm; (3) read `v` after the branch and return it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). Do not pre-initialize `v` to a placeholder value; if the language requires a placeholder, that requirement is itself the observation.
probes.measured_fragment: The declaration, the two-way branch with both assignments, and the final read/return.

probes.title: Explicitly uninitialized fixed-size buffer
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express genuinely uninitialized bulk storage (as opposed to zero/default-filled storage), and whether the fragment tells the reader which of the two it got.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) obtain storage for exactly 16 elements of an unsigned 8-bit integer element type whose contents are NOT specified to be zero or any other value — i.e. request uninitialized storage using the language's documented mechanism for doing so; (2) write the value 1 into element 0; (3) read element 0 and return it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no documented way to obtain uninitialized storage and always zero-or-default-initializes, the fragment must instead obtain the default-initialized 16-element buffer and the probe is scored by the rubric — the substituted fragment is still written and measured.
probes.measured_fragment: The buffer acquisition, the single write, and the single read/return.

probes.title: In-place increment of a scalar variable
probes.intent: Measure the minimal surface form of scalar mutation and how much of mutability, target identity, overflow behavior and side-effect scope is recoverable from that single form.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared, already-initialized mutable local `x` of a signed 32-bit integer type, write exactly one statement or expression that increases `x` by 1 in place, using the language's ordinary in-place update form (compound assignment or increment operator, whichever is the normal choice in that language). The measured fragment is that single statement/expression. The declaration of `x` is given context, not part of the fragment.
probes.measured_fragment: The single update statement/expression.

probes.title: In-place element mutation of a growable sequence through a name
probes.intent: Measure whether mutation through an aggregate binding is locally evident, and whether the reader can tell that the change is observable through the original name rather than through a copy.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `xs` bound to a growable, ordered, integer-element sequence (the language's normal dynamic list/vector/array-list type) already holding at least 3 elements: write exactly one statement that sets the element at index 1 to the value 42 in place, such that a subsequent read of `xs` element 1 through the name `xs` observes 42. The measured fragment is that single statement. Do not rebuild or reassign `xs`.
probes.measured_fragment: The single element-assignment statement.

probes.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
probes.title: Writable alias to an existing scalar local
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can create a second name that writes the SAME scalar storage as an existing local, and how explicitly the surface form announces the writable alias and its dereference.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a mutable local `x` of a signed 32-bit integer type initialized to 1; (2) introduce a second name `r` that denotes the SAME storage as `x` and through which `x` can be written (a writable alias / mutable reference / pointer / inout binding — whatever the language provides); (3) write the value 9 through `r`; (4) read `x` (not `r`) and return it, so the observable result is 9. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). If the language has no documented way for two names in the same scope to denote the same scalar storage with write access, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason.
probes.measured_fragment: All four statements.

probes.family: 4. aliasing, references, borrowing, addressing, and dereferencing where applicable
probes.title: Non-copying read-only view onto an existing sequence
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express a borrow/view that does not copy the elements, and whether the surface form tells the reader that (a) no copy occurred and (b) writes through the view are or are not possible.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body, given an already-declared local `xs` holding a growable integer sequence with at least 3 elements: (1) introduce a name `v` that denotes a read-only view/reference over `xs`'s existing elements WITHOUT copying those elements; (2) read element 0 through `v` and return it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2). The fragment must be one from which a reader can determine, without running the program, both whether the elements were copied and whether a write through `v` would be accepted. If the language offers no non-copying read-only view, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason.
probes.measured_fragment: The view introduction and the read/return.

probes.title: REQUIRED spec-6.1.4.B probe — ordinary bare call site f(x)
probes.intent: Spec 6.1.4.B mandates this probe. Measure how many materially distinct aliasing/mutation outcomes for the caller's argument remain possible from the ORDINARY call-site expression alone, before consulting the callee's signature or body.
probes.canonical_task: Given, as context declared ELSEWHERE in the same compilation unit and NOT part of the measured fragment, an ordinary one-parameter function `f` whose single parameter has the language's normal growable-integer-sequence type and whose declaration uses the plainest parameter form a normal author would write. Inside a function body write exactly: (1) a local `x` bound to a growable integer sequence containing the elements 1, 2, 3; (2) a call of `f` on `x` written with the language's plainest ordinary call-site syntax — literally the form an author writes when they merely want to pass `x` to `f`, with NO extra sigil, address-of, borrow marker, copy, clone, wrapper, annotation, or modifier at the argument position; (3) a read of element 0 of `x` after the call, returned as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). SCORING NOTE, binding for metric B: the determinacy count for this probe is the number of materially distinct outcomes for `x` and for the elements `x` denotes — including at minimum {callee cannot observe caller's object at all; callee may read but not write it; callee may write elements observable through `x`; callee may replace/resize the sequence observable through `x`; callee may retain the alias beyond the call; a copy was made so no caller-visible change is possible} — that remain compatible with the call-site expression in (2) ALONE, without consulting `f`'s declaration, signature, documentation, or body.
probes.measured_fragment: The local binding of `x`, the bare call expression, and the post-call read/return. `f`'s own declaration is explicitly excluded from the token count and is counted as a non-local lookup for metric C.

probes.title: REQUIRED spec-6.1.4.B counterpart — explicit reference / borrow / address / inout / dereference form
probes.intent: Spec 6.1.4.B mandates that the explicit writable-alias passing forms be tested SEPARATELY from the bare call site. Measure how determinately the language's dedicated forms announce, at the call site and/or the parameter, that the callee receives writable access to the caller's storage.
probes.canonical_task: Express all of: (1) a one-parameter function `g` that takes writable access to a caller-owned signed 32-bit integer variable and, in its body, sets that variable to 7 (the body is exactly that one assignment); (2) inside a caller function, a mutable local `x` of the same integer type initialized to 1; (3) a call of `g` on `x` using whatever explicit reference / borrow / address-of / inout / pointer / dereference form the language REQUIRES or CONVENTIONALLY USES for this purpose, at the call site and/or in `g`'s parameter declaration; (4) a read of `x` after the call, returned as the fragment's result, whose value must be 7. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4), i.e. for this probe `g`'s declaration and body ARE inside the boundary, because the explicit form may live there. If the language provides no documented way for a callee to write a caller's scalar local variable, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason (wrapping the integer in a mutable container/object is NOT an acceptable substitute for FULL — see rubric criterion P-a).
probes.measured_fragment: `g`'s full declaration and body, the caller's local, the call, and the post-call read/return.

probes.title: Returning an element out of an aggregate — value or shared storage?
probes.intent: Measure whether the reader can tell from the fragment whether a returned result is an independent value or continues to share storage with the aggregate it came from, and whether a copy/move/allocation occurs at the return.
probes.canonical_task: Express all of: (1) a function `mid` with one parameter of the language's normal growable-integer-sequence type, whose body returns the element at index 1 of that parameter; (2) at a call site, a local `xs` bound to such a sequence containing 1, 2, 3; (3) `let y = mid(xs)` in that language's normal form; (4) return `y`. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). A reader must be able to determine, from the fragment, whether `y` is independent of `xs` and whether the return performed a copy, a move, or shared a reference.
probes.measured_fragment: The full function declaration and body, the call site binding, and the final return.

probes.title: Two results from one call
probes.intent: Measure how the language returns more than one result at once and how much of the result types, independence and destructuring is recoverable at the call site.
probes.canonical_task: Express all of: (1) a function `divmod2` taking two signed 32-bit integer parameters `a` and `b` and producing BOTH the integer quotient a/b and the integer remainder a%b from a single call, using the language's normal multiple-result mechanism (tuple, multiple return values, a small record/struct/data class, or out-parameters — whichever is that language's normal choice; no third-party package); (2) a call site that binds the two results to two separate local names `q` and `r` in one binding construct if the language has one; (3) return q + r. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3).
probes.measured_fragment: The full function declaration and body, the binding call site, and the final return.

probes.title: Fused multiply-add expression on fixed-width signed integers
probes.intent: Measure how much of operand type, result type, precedence, evaluation and numeric behavior a reader recovers from a plain arithmetic expression.
probes.canonical_task: Given three already-declared, already-initialized locals `a`, `b`, `c`, all of the same signed 32-bit integer type: write exactly one statement binding a new local `r` to the value of the expression a * b + c, using the language's ordinary multiplication and addition operators and the language's ordinary precedence (no redundant parentheses). The measured fragment is that single binding statement. The three operand declarations are given context, not part of the fragment.
probes.measured_fragment: The single binding statement.

probes.title: Integer division, remainder, and real division of the same operands
probes.intent: Measure how the language distinguishes truncating/flooring integer division from real division, what the remainder operator does with negative operands, and how much of that is visible at the operator.
probes.canonical_task: Given two already-declared, already-initialized locals `a` and `b` of the same signed 32-bit integer type, where `a` may be negative: write exactly three binding statements, in this order: (1) bind `q` to the integer quotient of `a` and `b` using the language's ordinary integer division operator or the normal integer-division form if the ordinary operator is not integer division; (2) bind `m` to the remainder of `a` and `b` using the language's ordinary remainder/modulo operator; (3) bind `d` to the 64-bit floating-point division of `a` by `b`, performing whatever conversion the language requires to obtain a floating-point result, written the way a normal author would write it. The measured fragment is those three statements. A reader must be able to determine the rounding direction of (1) and the sign of (2) when `a` is negative.
probes.measured_fragment: The three binding statements.

probes.family: 8. integer overflow, division-by-zero, and other numeric edge behavior
probes.title: Adding one at the signed 32-bit maximum, with the overflow outcome determinable at the site
probes.intent: Measure whether the language lets the author SELECT and LOCALLY SIGNAL the overflow discipline (wrap, trap, saturate, error value, promote), and whether the outcome is recoverable from the fragment without knowing compiler flags or build mode.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a local `m` of a signed 32-bit integer type initialized to the maximum representable value of that type, written using the language's standard named maximum if one exists; (2) compute `m + 1` and bind the outcome to a local `o`, using the language's operation whose overflow behavior is determined BY THE OPERATION ITSELF — i.e. if the language provides explicit wrapping / checked / saturating / trapping arithmetic operations in the language or its standard library, use the one that makes the behavior explicit at the site; if it provides only the plain operator, use the plain operator; (3) produce `o` (or, if the chosen operation yields a wrapped optional/error, produce the fallback integer 0 on the exceptional case) as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). A reader must be able to state, from the fragment alone, exactly what happens at the overflow, without consulting the build recipe.
probes.measured_fragment: The three statements.

probes.family: 8. integer overflow, division-by-zero, and other numeric edge behavior
probes.title: Integer division where the divisor may be zero
probes.intent: Measure how determinately the zero-divisor outcome is expressed at the division site and whether the language offers a form that turns it into a value rather than an unsignalled trap.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body, given already-declared locals `a` and `b` of the same signed 32-bit integer type where `b` may be 0 at runtime: write the fragment that binds a local `q` to the result of dividing `a` by `b` in a form that makes the zero-divisor outcome determinable at the site — preferring, in this fixed order of preference, (i) a standard checked-division operation that yields an optional/error value, (ii) an explicit local guard on `b == 0` that selects a fallback integer 0, (iii) the plain division operator if neither (i) nor (ii) is idiomatic in that language; and then producing `q` (with 0 substituted for the exceptional case) as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is the whole binding construct plus the final production of `q`. `a` and `b`'s declarations are given context.
probes.measured_fragment: The division/guard construct and the production of `q`.

probes.title: String equality — identity or contents?
probes.intent: Measure whether the fragment tells the reader whether the language's ordinary equality operator on the normal text-string type compares object identity or character contents, and whether user-defined or dynamic equality could be dispatched here.
probes.canonical_task: Given two already-declared locals `s1` and `s2` of the language's ordinary text-string type, both holding runtime-produced strings that may be distinct objects with identical contents: write exactly one statement binding a new local `eq` to the boolean result of comparing `s1` and `s2` the way a normal author compares two strings for sameness of contents in that language. The measured fragment is that single statement. A reader must be able to determine, from the statement alone, whether contents or identity are compared.
probes.measured_fragment: The single binding statement.

probes.title: Ascending sort of a sequence, plus a scalar ordering comparison
probes.intent: Measure how the language expresses a total order, whether the ordering used by the standard sort is locally evident, and whether the sort mutates in place or produces a new sequence.
probes.canonical_task: Write exactly two statements: (1) sort an already-declared local `xs` (growable integer sequence, at least 3 elements) into ascending order using the language's standard ordering facility, with no user-supplied comparator if the language supplies a default order for integers; (2) bind a new local `lt` to the boolean value of whether already-declared integer `a` is strictly less than already-declared integer `b`, using the ordinary comparison operator. The measured fragment is those two statements. A reader must be able to determine from (1) whether `xs` itself was reordered in place or a new sequence was produced, and whether any allocation occurred.
probes.measured_fragment: The two statements.

probes.title: Narrowing a 64-bit signed integer to 32 bits
probes.intent: Measure how explicitly the language marks a lossy narrowing conversion and how determinately the out-of-range outcome is expressed at the conversion site.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `big` of a signed 64-bit integer type whose runtime value may exceed the 32-bit signed range: write the fragment that produces a local `small` of a signed 32-bit integer type from `big`, written the way a normal author would write this conversion in that language, and then produces `small` as the fragment's result. If the language's standard library offers a conversion that reports out-of-range as an optional/error value, prefer it and substitute the fallback integer 0 for the out-of-range case. The measured fragment is the conversion binding plus the production of `small`. A reader must be able to state from the fragment what happens when the value does not fit: truncate, wrap, trap, saturate, yield an error value, or be statically rejected.
probes.measured_fragment: The conversion binding and the production of `small`.

probes.title: Mixed integer and floating-point arithmetic
probes.intent: Measure whether a mixed-type arithmetic expression reveals, at the operator, which operand changed representation and what the result type is — the classic site of implicit conversion.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `i` of a signed 32-bit integer type and an already-declared local `d` of a 64-bit floating-point type: write exactly one statement binding a new local `sum` to the sum of `i` and `d`, written the way a normal author would write it in that language (including any conversion the language requires to be written explicitly, and omitting any the language performs implicitly). The measured fragment is that single statement. A reader must be able to determine the static type of `sum` and which operand's representation changed.
probes.measured_fragment: The single binding statement.

probes.title: Indexed read with a possibly-out-of-range runtime index
probes.intent: Measure how determinately the out-of-range outcome of an ordinary indexing expression is expressed at the index site.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `xs` (growable integer sequence, 3 elements) and an already-declared local `i` of a signed integer type whose runtime value may be outside 0..2: write the fragment that reads the element of `xs` at index `i`, binds it to a local `e`, and produces `e` as the fragment's result, written the way a normal author writes an indexed read in that language. If the language's standard library offers a non-trapping indexed read yielding an optional/error value, ALSO write that form as a second, separately measured variant labelled `F11.P1.checked` and use the fallback integer 0 for the absent case; the primary measured fragment remains the ordinary form. A reader must be able to state, from the primary fragment, the out-of-range behavior: trap/panic, thrown exception, optional/error value, undefined behavior, silent clamp, or silent default value.
probes.measured_fragment: The indexed read binding and the production of `e`. The optional `.checked` variant is measured and reported separately but does not change this probe's capability_points.

probes.title: Sub-range of a sequence — copy or shared storage?
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can express a sub-range at all, and whether the surface form reveals whether the sub-range copies elements or aliases the original's storage.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `xs` (growable integer sequence holding 10, 20, 30, 40, 50): write the fragment that produces a local `part` denoting exactly the elements at positions 1, 2 and 3 of `xs` (half-open range start=1, end=4), using the language's normal sub-range/slice/sub-list form, and then produces the element at position 0 of `part` (value 20) as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is the sub-range binding plus the production of the element. A reader must be able to determine from the fragment whether `part` copies the three elements or shares storage with `xs`, and whether a later write through `xs` would be observable through `part`.
probes.measured_fragment: The sub-range binding and the element production.

probes.title: Declared-absent optional integer with a default fallback
probes.intent: Measure whether optionality is expressed in the type, whether the absent case is constructible explicitly, and how the fallback is written.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) declare a local `o` whose type explicitly admits either a signed 32-bit integer or the absence of a value, and initialize it to the ABSENT case using the language's explicit absent-value form; (2) bind a local `n` of the plain signed 32-bit integer type to the contained value of `o` if present and to 0 if absent, using the language's standard default/fallback/coalescing form for optionals (not a hand-written if-statement, if the language provides such a form); (3) produce `n` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no type-level distinction between 'an integer' and 'possibly no integer', the fragment must still be written using whatever absent sentinel the language normally uses, and the probe is scored by the rubric.
probes.measured_fragment: The three statements.

probes.title: Optional-preserving transformation without an explicit conditional
probes.intent: Measure whether the language provides a standard optional-aware chaining/mapping operation and how locally evident the short-circuit on absence is.
probes.canonical_task: Given an already-declared local `o` of the possibly-absent-32-bit-integer type from F12.P1, and an already-declared unary function `h` taking a signed 32-bit integer and returning a signed 32-bit integer: write the fragment that binds a local `p`, of the same possibly-absent-integer type, to `h` applied to `o`'s contained value when present and to the absent case when `o` is absent — WITHOUT writing an explicit `if`/`switch`/`match` statement, using instead the language's standard optional-aware chaining, mapping, or safe-call operation if it has one. Then produce a plain integer result: `p`'s contained value if present, else 0. The measured fragment is the binding of `p` plus the final production. If the language has no such operation, write the explicit conditional and score by the rubric.
probes.measured_fragment: The binding of `p` and the final production.

probes.family: 13. errors, failure values, exceptions, and propagation
probes.title: Propagating a standard-library parse failure to the caller
probes.intent: Measure whether a function's declared interface reveals that it can fail, and how visible the propagation point is in the body.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete function `parse_twice` taking one parameter `s` of the language's ordinary text-string type, which: (1) converts `s` to a signed 32-bit integer using the language's STANDARD library string-to-integer conversion, an operation that can fail on malformed input; (2) on failure, propagates that failure to its own caller WITHOUT handling it, using the language's normal propagation mechanism (thrown exception, error-returning propagation operator, explicit early return of the error value, etc.); (3) on success, returns twice the parsed value. The function's declared result type and declared failure behavior must be whatever the language requires or conventionally writes. The measured fragment is the function's complete declaration and body. A reader must be able to determine from the declaration alone whether calling this function can fail, and from the body where the failure can leave.
probes.measured_fragment: The complete function declaration and body.

probes.family: 13. errors, failure values, exceptions, and propagation
probes.title: Locally handling a failure and recovering with a fallback
probes.intent: Measure how the language expresses local recovery, and whether the fragment reveals the control-flow and cleanup consequences of taking the failure path.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) call the fallible standard-library string-to-integer conversion on an already-declared text-string local `s`; (2) handle failure LOCALLY, binding a local `n` of the plain signed 32-bit integer type to the parsed value on success and to the fallback value 0 on failure, using the language's normal local-handling construct (catch block, match/switch on the result value, if-error form, try-with-default, recover, etc.); (3) produce `n` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). A reader must be able to determine which operations inside the construct are protected, and whether any cleanup or unwinding occurs on the failure path.
probes.measured_fragment: The whole handling construct and the production of `n`.

probes.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
probes.title: Declaring a closed two-alternative type with per-alternative payloads
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can declare a CLOSED set of alternatives each carrying its own differently-shaped payload, and whether the closedness and the payloads are evident in the declaration.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a declaration of a type named `Shape` with EXACTLY two alternatives and no others — `Circle`, carrying a single 64-bit floating-point field `r`, and `Rect`, carrying two 64-bit floating-point fields `w` and `h` — where the set of alternatives is closed, i.e. the language's own rules prevent code elsewhere from adding a third alternative; (2) a statement constructing a `Circle` with r = 2.0 and binding it to a local `s` whose static type is `Shape` (not `Circle`). The measured fragment is (1)+(2). If the language cannot express a closed alternative set, express the nearest standard construct (e.g. an open class hierarchy, or a tagged record with a discriminant field) and score by the rubric.
probes.measured_fragment: The type declaration and the construction/binding statement.

probes.family: 14. alternatives / sum / variant types and dispatch over alternatives
probes.title: Exhaustive dispatch over the alternatives
probes.intent: Measure whether the language checks exhaustiveness of alternative handling and whether the dispatch construct reveals the payload binding and the fate of an unhandled alternative.
probes.canonical_task: Given the `Shape` type and the local `s` from F14.P1: write the fragment that computes the area of `s` by dispatching over its alternatives — for `Circle`, 3.141592653589793 * r * r; for `Rect`, w * h — binding the result to a 64-bit floating-point local `area` and producing `area` as the fragment's result. Use the language's normal dispatch-over-alternatives construct (pattern match, switch over cases, sealed-when, virtual method, visitor — whichever is that language's normal choice for a closed alternative set). Write NO default/else/catch-all arm. The measured fragment is the dispatch construct and the production of `area`. A reader must be able to determine whether the language guarantees all alternatives are covered and what happens at runtime if one is not.
probes.measured_fragment: The dispatch construct and the production of `area`.

probes.title: One unconstrained generic function used at two element types
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can abstract over an element type once and reuse it at two types, and whether the type relationship between argument and result is recoverable statically from the declaration.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a single function `first` that, for an ARBITRARY element type T, takes a sequence whose elements are of type T and returns the element at index 0, with a declared result type that is T (not a universal/dynamic/erased-to-Object type, if the language can express that relationship); (2) a call `first` on a sequence of signed 32-bit integers containing 1, 2, 3, bound to a local `a`; (3) a call `first` on a sequence of text strings containing "x", "y", bound to a local `b`; (4) production of a result combining both, namely the text-string concatenation of the textual rendering of `a` and the value of `b`. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). If the language has no parametric mechanism and only a universal dynamic type, write the nearest standard form and score by the rubric.
probes.measured_fragment: The generic function declaration and body, both call sites, and the combining production.

probes.title: Constrained generic function over an orderable element type
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can state, at the generic declaration, the requirement its body relies on, and whether the constraint is checked at the declaration or only at instantiation.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a single function `max_of` that, for an arbitrary element type T CONSTRAINED to be ordered/comparable by the language's own standard ordering abstraction (trait, interface, protocol, type class, concept, bound, or equivalent), takes two arguments of type T and returns the greater of them, using the ordinary comparison form in its body; (2) one call of `max_of` on the signed 32-bit integers 3 and 5, bound to a local `m`, and production of `m` as the fragment's result. The constraint must be written at the declaration if the language supports declaration-site constraints. The measured fragment is (1)+(2). If the language has no way to express the constraint, write the nearest standard form and score by the rubric; record explicitly whether misuse is diagnosed at the generic's declaration or only at the call site.
probes.measured_fragment: The constrained generic declaration and body, plus the single call and production.

probes.title: Build a growable integer sequence and sum it by iteration
probes.intent: Measure the cost and clarity of constructing a sequence and traversing it, and whether allocation, element mutability and iteration-time modification rules are evident.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) construct a growable, ordered sequence of signed 32-bit integers containing exactly the elements 1, 2, 3, bound to a local `xs`, using the language's normal literal or builder form for that type; (2) bind a local `total` of the same integer type to the sum of all of `xs`'s elements, computed by ITERATING over `xs` with the language's normal iteration construct (a loop, or a standard fold/reduce/sum operation from the standard library — whichever a normal author would use); (3) produce `total` as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3).
probes.measured_fragment: The three statements.

probes.title: String-keyed map: iterate entries, and look up a missing key
probes.intent: Measure whether iteration-order guarantees and lookup-miss behavior are evident from the fragment, both classic sources of hidden semantics.
probes.canonical_task: Inside a function body: (1) construct a mapping from text-string keys to signed 32-bit integer values containing exactly one entry, key "a" mapped to 1, bound to a local `mp`, using the language's normal map/dictionary type and normal construction form; (2) bind a local `total` to the sum of all VALUES in `mp`, computed by iterating over its entries with the language's normal entry-iteration construct; (3) bind a local `miss` of the plain signed 32-bit integer type to the result of looking up the key "b" (which is absent) in `mp`, substituting 0 for the absent case, written the way a normal author writes a lookup-with-default in that language; (4) produce total + miss as the fragment's result. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3)+(4). A reader must be able to determine whether iteration order is specified, and what an unguarded lookup of an absent key would do.
probes.measured_fragment: The four statements.

probes.family: 17. resource management, ownership, lifetime, destruction, or equivalent cleanup semantics
probes.title: Scoped file handle released on every exit path
probes.intent: Measure how the language guarantees release of an OS resource at scope exit including on the failure path, and whether the release point is evident at the acquisition site.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete function `read_all` with no parameters that: (1) opens the file named "data.txt" for reading using only the standard library (this can fail); (2) reads its entire contents into a text-string local `text`; (3) guarantees that the file handle is released when the enclosing scope ends, INCLUDING when step (2) fails, using the language's normal scoped-cleanup mechanism (destructor/RAII, defer, with-statement, using/try-with-resources, drop at end of scope, finally — whichever is normal in that language); (4) returns the length in bytes of `text`, and propagates or handles the open/read failure in whatever way that language's mechanism requires. The measured fragment is the complete function declaration and body. A reader must be able to determine WHERE the release happens and that it happens exactly once on every exit path.
probes.measured_fragment: The complete function declaration and body.

probes.family: 17. resource management, ownership, lifetime, destruction, or equivalent cleanup semantics
probes.title: User-defined type with a deterministic end-of-lifetime cleanup hook
probes.intent: Measure whether a user-defined type can attach a cleanup action that runs deterministically and exactly once at the end of a value's lifetime, and whether the fragment reveals where that point is.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a declaration of a user-defined type `Handle` holding a single signed 32-bit integer field `id`, which performs a cleanup action — incrementing an already-declared module-level counter `released` by 1 — EXACTLY ONCE and DETERMINISTICALLY when a value of the type reaches the end of its lifetime, using the language's own end-of-lifetime hook (destructor, drop, deinit, close-on-scope-exit, dispose pattern, etc.); (2) a block that creates a `Handle` with id = 1 bound to a local, and then ends; (3) after that block, a read of `released` produced as the fragment's result, whose value must be 1. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no deterministic end-of-lifetime hook and only nondeterministic reclamation, express the nearest standard construct (e.g. an explicit close/dispose invoked by a scoped construct) and score by the rubric; if the language has no standard scoped construct either, record NONE.
probes.measured_fragment: The type declaration including the cleanup hook, the block, and the final read/production.

probes.title: Importing and using one standard-library console-output facility
probes.intent: Measure whether the fragment reveals which external names enter scope and from where — the dependency-boundary transparency of a single import.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) whatever declaration is required in that language to make the standard console/text-output facility available in this compilation unit (an import, include, use, module reference, or nothing if the facility is available without one); (2) exactly one statement that writes the text "x" followed by a newline to standard output using that facility. The measured fragment is (1)+(2). A reader must be able to determine which names the declaration introduces into scope and which unit provides them.
probes.measured_fragment: The import/include declaration (if any) and the single output statement.

probes.title: A code unit with one exported and one private item, used from outside
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can draw an enforced visibility boundary around a unit and whether that boundary is evident at both the declaration and the external use site.
probes.canonical_task: Express: (1) a single unit of code (module, namespace, package, or file-level unit — the language's normal grouping construct) named `util`, containing exactly two items: an EXPORTED/PUBLIC function `pub_add` taking two signed 32-bit integers and returning their sum plus the result of `secret()`, and a NON-EXPORTED/PRIVATE function `secret` taking no parameters and returning 1, where the language's own rules prevent `secret` from being referenced from outside `util`; (2) from OUTSIDE `util`, a call `util.pub_add(2, 3)` written with whatever qualification that language requires, bound to a local and produced as the fragment's result (value 6). The measured fragment is (1)+(2). If the language cannot enforce the private boundary within a single compilation unit as configured by the frozen recipe, express the nearest standard form (including a second file if that is the language's normal unit granularity — a second file is permitted here and is NOT a third-party dependency) and score by the rubric.
probes.measured_fragment: The unit declaration with both items, and the external qualified call with its binding and production.

probes.family: 19. concurrency / asynchronous execution where the language supports it
probes.title: Two concurrent computations joined into one result
probes.intent: Measure whether the language has a standard way to run two computations concurrently and deterministically combine their results, and whether the concurrency, the join point and the failure modes are evident.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that: (1) starts TWO independent units of concurrent or asynchronous execution, the first computing the integer 20 and the second computing the integer 22, using ONLY the language's standard concurrency/async facility as shipped with the frozen toolchain (thread, task, goroutine, coroutine, async function plus its standard runtime, actor, future/promise, structured-concurrency group); (2) waits for BOTH to finish; (3) binds a local `sum` to the sum of their two results (42) and produces it. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3), including whatever launcher/runtime/entry wrapper the language requires to run async code, but excluding a plain non-async `main` wrapper. If the language has NO standard concurrency or asynchronous execution facility at all, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason. A single-threaded cooperative async facility DOES count and must be recorded as such.
probes.measured_fragment: The launch of both units, the join, and the combining production, plus any required async runtime entry construct.

probes.family: 19. concurrency / asynchronous execution where the language supports it
probes.title: Race-free increment of shared state from two concurrent units
probes.intent: Measure whether the language and its standard library let the author express a documented race-free discipline over shared mutable state, and whether that discipline is evident at the mutation site.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that: (1) establishes a single shared signed 64-bit integer counter initialized to 0; (2) from TWO concurrent or asynchronous units of execution, increments that counter 1000 times each, using ONLY standard-library or language-level synchronization (mutex/lock, atomic operation, channel serialization, actor isolation, or a language-enforced exclusion rule) such that the program is DOCUMENTED BY THE LANGUAGE to be free of data races; (3) waits for both, then produces the counter's final value, which must be exactly 2000. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3) including the synchronization construct and any required async runtime entry construct. If the language has no standard concurrency facility, no fragment is written; record NONE. If the language has concurrency but its semantics make this program race-free WITHOUT any explicit synchronization construct (e.g. a global interpreter lock, single-threaded event loop, or compiler-enforced exclusion), write the fragment that way and record exactly which language rule supplies the guarantee.
probes.measured_fragment: The shared-state establishment, both concurrent increment loops with their synchronization, the join, and the final production.

probes.title: Calling a C library function across the FFI boundary
probes.intent: Measure whether the language can reach a platform C function using only its own standard mechanism, and whether the fragment reveals the foreignness, the ABI, the argument representation and the safety status of the call.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that: (1) declares the C standard-library function with the C signature `int abs(int)` as an external/foreign function, using ONLY the language's built-in FFI/interoperability mechanism as shipped with the frozen toolchain — no third-party package, no separate binding generator, no separate build system step beyond the frozen recipe (linking against the platform C library that the frozen recipe already links by default is permitted); (2) calls it once with the argument -3; (3) binds the returned C `int` to a local of the language's corresponding signed 32-bit integer type and produces it as the fragment's result, whose value must be 3. The measured fragment is (1)+(2)+(3). If the language has no built-in FFI mechanism meeting these conditions, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason. A reader must be able to determine from the fragment that the call crosses a foreign boundary, what calling convention/ABI is assumed, and whether the call is marked unsafe or unchecked.
probes.measured_fragment: The foreign declaration, the call, and the binding/production.

probes.title: Exporting a function with C ABI and a stable unmangled symbol
probes.intent: Measure the OUTBOUND interoperability direction: whether the language can publish a function callable from C with a stable, unmangled symbol name and the C calling convention, using only its own standard mechanism.
probes.canonical_task: Express a complete fragment that declares a function taking two C-`int`-compatible signed 32-bit integers `a` and `b` and returning their sum, which is (1) compiled with the C calling convention / C ABI, and (2) exported under the exact, unmangled external symbol name `add2`, using ONLY the language's built-in mechanism for C-compatible export (extern "C", no_mangle plus extern, export, cdecl attribute, JNI-style external linkage, or equivalent) with no third-party package and no separate code-generation step. The measured fragment is that declaration, its annotations/attributes, and its body. Verification is objective and MANDATORY: build the enclosing unit with the frozen recipe for that language and confirm with the platform symbol lister (`nm`) that a symbol whose name is exactly `add2` (allowing only the platform's uniform leading-underscore convention) is present and defined. If the language cannot produce such a symbol with only its standard mechanism, no fragment is written; record NONE with the reason and with the `nm` evidence.
probes.measured_fragment: The exported function's annotations, declaration and body.

spec_6_1_4_B_required_probe_mapping.note: Spec 6.1.4.B requires BOTH: an ordinary call-site expression equivalent to f(x) measured for how many materially distinct aliasing/mutation outcomes remain possible from the call-site syntax ALONE (F05.P1), and a SEPARATE probe of the explicit reference/borrow/address/dereference/writable-alias forms the language provides (F05.P2). Both exist and are scored independently.
spec_6_1_4_B_required_probe_mapping.glyph_neutrality_rule: Per spec 6.1.4.B, no probe awards or removes points merely because a language spells something with the glyph `&` (or `*`, `ref`, `inout`, `var`, `borrow`, or any other token). Score only the semantic determinacy conveyed by the complete surface form, evaluated identically for all 10 languages.

support_rubric._purpose: Frozen before any measurement (spec 6.1.7 item 4). Applied identically to all 10 languages, probe by probe.
support_rubric._baseline_condition: Support is credited ONLY when the probe can be expressed using documented language features or the language's normal standard runtime/library as shipped with the frozen toolchain, WITHOUT benchmark-specific external packages and WITHOUT code generation. Third-party packages, package-manager fetches, binding generators, separate build systems, hand-written assembly, and toolchains outside the frozen environment all disqualify.

observable_criteria: F-1. Every explicitly numbered sub-requirement in the probe's canonical_task is delivered by the fragment, with none dropped, weakened, or substituted.
F-2. The fragment uses only documented language features and the standard runtime/library bundled with the frozen toolchain version for that language.
F-3. The fragment builds (where the language has a build step) and runs to completion under the frozen recipe for that language, unmodified, producing the stated observable result.
F-4. No third-party package, no package-manager dependency, no code-generation step, and no compiler/runtime flag beyond the frozen recipe is required.
F-5. Every fact kind listed in semantic_facts_expected is DETERMINABLE for that language at the probe (possibly requiring non-local lookup — locality cost is metric C's business, not coverage's).

F-6. The language's own documentation does not mark the mechanism used as unsafe, deprecated, discouraged, or reflective. (Mechanisms the language documents as a first-class facility that merely requires an `unsafe`/`unchecked` keyword — e.g. FFI — are NOT disqualified by this criterion, because the keyword is the documented normal way to use the facility; see P-d for what is.)

At least one numbered sub-requirement of canonical_task IS delivered, AND at least one of the following observable conditions holds. The condition(s) that applied MUST be recorded by letter in the results record for that (probe, language) pair:

P-a. SUBSTITUTED WEAKER MECHANISM. The observable behavior is achieved only by substituting a weaker but standard mechanism that drops a named sub-requirement — e.g. an open class hierarchy where the task demands a closed alternative set; a mutable container/object wrapper where the task demands writable access to a caller's scalar local; a runtime-checked cast where the task demands a statically expressed type relationship; an unconstrained generic where the task demands a declaration-site constraint; a copying slice where the task demands the reader be able to tell copy from share and the language offers only one.

P-b. FLAG OR MODE OUTSIDE THE FROZEN RECIPE. The behavior requires a compiler/runtime flag, mode, pragma, or preview/experimental switch beyond the frozen recipe, but that switch ships with the frozen toolchain and needs no additional download.

P-c. GUARANTEE NOT DOCUMENTED. The standard library provides the shape of the behavior, but the specific GUARANTEE the canonical_task names (deterministic cleanup point, specified iteration order, documented race-freedom, exactly-once execution, non-copying view, closed alternative set) is documented as unspecified, implementation-defined, or best-effort, so the fragment can only approximate it.

P-d. DOCUMENTED ESCAPE HATCH. The only expression available is via a mechanism the language's own documentation marks as unsafe-and-discouraged, deprecated, internal, or reflective (e.g. reflection to reach a private member, a finalizer the language documents as not to be relied upon, an internal/unstable API), while still shipping in the standard distribution.

P-e. EXTRA COMPILATION UNIT OR ENTRY SCAFFOLD. The probe is expressible only by adding a structural scaffold the canonical_task did not ask for and that is required purely by the language's unit granularity (e.g. a second file, a wrapper class, an explicit async runtime block where the task asked for none). NOTE: F18.P2 and F19.P1 explicitly permit their respective scaffolds, so P-e does NOT apply to those two probes.
PARTIAL.no_double_penalty_rule: Multiple applicable PARTIAL conditions do not stack. PARTIAL is a single 0.5 factor however many letters apply. Record all applicable letters for audit.

observable_criteria: N-1. The language provides NO documented standard way to deliver ANY numbered sub-requirement of the canonical_task; or
N-2. The only available expression requires a third-party package, an external code generator, a separate build system or toolchain outside the frozen environment, or hand-written assembly; or
N-3. The fragment cannot be made to build or run under the frozen recipe (and the probe did not ask for a statically-rejected case); or
N-4. The probe's own canonical_task explicitly directs that no fragment be written for a language lacking the mechanism (F04.P1, F04.P2, F05.P2, F17.P2-final-clause, F19.P1, F19.P2, F20.P1, F20.P2).

Every NONE MUST carry a written justification citing the specific language rule or documentation that makes the capability unavailable, plus, where applicable, the exact build/run error or `nm` output observed.

deterministic_tie_break.question: Does the fragment observably deliver EVERY explicitly numbered sub-requirement in the probe's canonical_task, under the frozen recipe, with only documented standard features?
deterministic_tie_break.binding: This question is the sole arbiter. If two reviewers disagree, they must disagree about an observable fact (does it build? does the documentation say X?), not about a judgement of quality, elegance, or idiom.

evidence_required_per_pair: the fragment source text (or the NONE justification)
the exact build command and its exit status
the exact run command and the observed stdout/exit status against the canonical_task's stated result
the support level, the applicable P-letter(s) or N-reason, and a citation to the language documentation relied on
adjudication_and_audit.no_post_hoc_adjustment: Support levels are assigned from this rubric before any Q-metric aggregation and are not revised after coverage totals or rankings are seen (spec 6.1.7, 32).

interaction_with_quality_metrics.rule: Metrics A (Semantic Density), B (Semantic Determinacy), C (Semantic Locality) and D (Hidden Semantic Cost) are computed over the probes for which a fragment exists, i.e. probes scored FULL or PARTIAL for that language. Probes scored NONE contribute no fragment and therefore no tokens, no fact counts, no branching counts, no lookup counts and no hidden-behavior counts.
interaction_with_quality_metrics.metric_E_denominator: Per spec 6.1.4.E, Capability Efficiency divides counted semantic-complexity units by the number of SUPPORTED capability points, i.e. sum over probes of capability_points * support_factor. This is the same numerator quantity used for Capability Coverage.
interaction_with_quality_metrics.anti_gaming_note: Because NONE probes are excluded from A-D but retained in the coverage denominator (see na_policy), a language cannot raise its quality score Q by failing to support hard probes without paying for it in C. The harmonic mean in spec 6.1.6 is what makes that trade unprofitable; this is intentional and applies identically to all 10 languages including Quidra.

capability_coverage.formula: C = 100 * (sum over the 40 probes of capability_points * support_factor) / total_fixed_capability_points
capability_coverage.reporting_requirement: Report C in aggregate AND broken down by each of the 20 capability families, using capability_points_by_family as each family's denominator (spec 6.1.5).

na_policy.note: Per spec section 26 and 6.1.1: for Semantic Compression Capability Coverage, an unsupported capability in this fixed universe REMAINS IN THE DENOMINATOR and therefore LOWERS coverage rather than becoming N/A. A missing capability must not escape scoring by being labeled N/A.
rules: NA-1. The denominator is fixed at 103 capability points for every one of the 10 languages, forever, regardless of what any language supports.
NA-2. A probe scored NONE for a language contributes 0 to that language's numerator and its full capability_points to the denominator. It is NOT marked N/A and it is NOT excluded.
NA-3. No probe may be deleted, reworded, or re-weighted because a language (including Quidra) lacks the capability (spec 32).

NA-4. The only legitimate N/A in Primary Evaluation 1 would be a measurement that cannot be taken for a reason unrelated to the language's capability — e.g. a metric-A token count for a probe where no fragment exists. That is handled by the interaction_with_quality_metrics rule above (exclusion from A-D), NOT by removing the probe from coverage.
NA-5. Every N/A actually recorded anywhere in Primary Evaluation 1 must carry a written reason naming which of these rules permits it (spec 26 final line).

NA-6. 'The language has no concept of X' is a NONE with a justification, never an N/A. This applies symmetrically: it is the expected outcome for several languages on F02.P2, F04.P1, F04.P2, F05.P2, F14.P1, F17.P2, F19.P1, F19.P2, F20.P1 and F20.P2, and the benchmark records it without commentary about which language is affected.

hard_family_honesty_declaration.statement: The five families where the 10 languages differ most (concurrency, FFI, ownership/lifetime/destruction, sum types, generics) are included at full weight and are NOT softened. They carry 30 of the 103 capability points (29.1%).
hard_family_honesty_declaration.expected_asymmetry_is_not_a_defect: It is expected and correct that some languages score NONE on several of these probes while others score FULL. That spread is the measurement, not a flaw in it. No probe in these families was weakened to reduce the spread, and none may be weakened afterwards.
hard_family_honesty_declaration.symmetry_check: Each of these families is scored by exactly the same rubric text and the same tie-break question as every other family. No family has a language-specific exemption, carve-out, or bonus.

downstream_obligations.freeze_order: Per spec 6.1.7 the remaining items must be frozen before measurement and are the subject of sibling methodology documents: (3) the hidden-behavior checklist, (5) token-counting and normalization rules, (6) per-probe validation against each real implementation or authoritative specification.
downstream_obligations.publication: Per spec 6.1.7, the probe definitions (this file), raw counts, scoring scripts, capability matrix, and normalization calculations must all be published in benchmark/.
